title: Hybrid latency-throughput tuner for prefill/decode scheduling
creator: Ava Chen
description:
Problem: Current prefill/decode arbitration uses coarse phase thresholds which either favors low-latency short requests or high-throughput long requests but cannot adapt to mixed workloads. We see tail latency regressions for interactive apps under bursty mixed traffic and inefficient kernel utilization for batchy throughput jobs.

Goals:
- Provide a runtime scheduler that dynamically tunes the fraction of GPU time allocated to prefill vs decode across queues to meet configurable latency SLOs while preserving throughput.
- Maintain fairness across customers/tenants and prevent starvation for long-running decode-heavy flows.
- Surface simple knobs for Console and APIs (percent latency SLO, min token-bandwidth, fairness window).

Design summary: "Hybrid Latency-Throughput Tuner" (HLTT) combines: (1) per-queue percentile-driven latency targets, (2) adaptive phase-split controller that adjusts prefill/decode budget ratios, and (3) kernel-hinting for batch composition.

Key ideas:
- Observability signal: track p50/p95/p99 for prefill-time and per-token decode latency per queue and per model-variant. Also track token-throughput and small/long request mix.
- Controller: for each scheduling window (configurable, default 500ms), compute the latency shortfall relative to target percentile. If prefill p95 > target, increase prefill fraction for next window by a delta proportional to shortfall and capped by max-step. Conversely, if decode p95 is above target, increment decode fraction. If both within targets, steer toward throughput-optimal split derived from offline kernel-util profiles.
- Kernel hints: annotate requests with expected decode length and attention-mode flags so batcher can coalesce compatible kernel paths (e.g., truncated attention kernels for short sequences, KV-optimized kernels for long-decoding flows). The controller uses kernel-cost models (latency per token per kernel) to compute throughput-optimal allocations when not constrained by latency.
- Fairness and starvation guards: each queue has a min guaranteed fraction (configurable) and a recovery credit so a queue that gets reduced below its min is guaranteed ramp-up to min over limited windows. Implement soft-proportional fairness via weighted deficit tokens where weight derives from SLA tier and recent service.

Runtime interface: new scheduler config (example YAML):
  scheduler:
    controller: hybrid-latency-throughput
    window_ms: 500
    target_latency_ms: 120  # p95 prefill latency target per queue
    max_step_fraction: 0.15
    min_fraction_per_queue: 0.05
    kernel_cost_profile: runtime-1.19/kernels/v1

Experiment plan:
- PoC locally with mixed replay (50% short interactive chat, 50% long generation batch) using workload-replayer and perf harness.
- Metric checks: p95 latency for interactive flows, token/sec throughput for batch flows, GPU utilization, tail-nanosecond jitter, fairness index (Jain's index over token/sec across queues).
- A/B: Compare current phase-threshold scheduler vs HLTT across 12h replay. Target: reduce interactive p95 by >=25% while keeping batch throughput within -10% of baseline and increasing average GPU utilization by >=8%.

Implementation notes:
- Controller runs in scheduler thread with lockless ring buffer for signals to avoid blocking hot path.
- Use exponential smoothing for percentiles to avoid oscillation.
- Add feature flag toggle to enable kernel hints; kernel-cost model pulled from offline benchmark table.

Acceptance criteria:
- Deterministic rollout gate: staging replay shows p95 improvement and throughput within tolerance.
- No regression on existing SLOs for dedicated customers in smoke tests.
- Integration tests for starvation guard and min-fraction enforcement included.

Risks and trade-offs:
- Oscillation risk if window_ms too small — mitigated by smoothing and max_step_fraction.
- Kernel hinting requires coordination with batcher; mislabels could reduce batching efficiency. Plan to fall back to conservative default kernel selection on mismatch.
- Complexity: additional knobs increase operational surface; prioritize good defaults and Console UX to visualize controller state.
